e-10897.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
e-10897.problem: Simplify the integral $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx$ using symmetry.
e-10897.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .
$$

Notice that $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function, we have

$$
\int_{-2}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx = 2 \int_{0}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx.
$$

e-10898.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
e-10898.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

- $\displaystyle \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 (e^x+e^{-x}) \, \textrm dx$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-\pi}^{2\pi} \sin(2x) \, \textrm dx$
e-10898.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x) = 4x^3$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =4(-x)^{3} \\  & =-4{x}^{3} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
\int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

- The function $g(x) = e^x+e^{-x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & ={e}^{(-x)}+{e}^{-(-x)} \\  & ={e}^{-x}+{e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}+{e}^{-x} \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x) = \sin(2x)$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form $\displaystyle \int_{-a}^a h(x)\,\textrm d x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. So, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

e-10911.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
e-10911.problem: Given that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = A,$ what is the value of $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 x\cos x  \, \textrm dx?$
e-10911.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Notice that $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
\int_{-1}^{1} x\cos x  \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =(-x)(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall the following:

  • a function f(x) is even if f(−x)=f(x)

  • a function f(x) is odd if f(−x)=−f(x)

Moreover, for any even function f(x), the graph of y=f(x) is symmetric across the y-axis, so we have ∫−aaf(x)dx=2∫0af(x)dx.

Notice that f(x)=xsin⁡x is an even function. Indeed, we have f(−x)=(−x)sin⁡(−x)=(−x)(−sin⁡x)=xsin⁡x=f(x).

So, because f(x)=xsin⁡x is an even function, we have ∫−ππxsin⁡xdx=2∫0πxsin⁡xdx.

content.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =(-x)(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\sqrt{(-x)^{2}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x.
$$

decision.explanation: The integrand is even because (-x)^4 e^{(-x)^2}=x^4 e^{x^2}. Therefore its integral over [-5,5] equals twice its integral over [0,5], giving option b.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{4}\,{e}^{(-x)^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}{x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{5}{x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{4}\,{e}^{(-x)^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}{x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{5}{x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =-2(-x)^{4} \\  & =-2{x}^{4} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x.

content.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =-2(-x)^{4} \\  & =-2{x}^{4} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Question 5
?

Simplify the integral ∫−1/21/2x21+x4dx using symmetry.

a
0
b
∫01x21+x4dx
c
12∫01/2x21+x4dx
d
12∫01x21+x4dx
e
2∫01/2x21+x4dx
Submit

decision.explanation: The integrand is even because (-x)^2/(1+(-x)^4)=x^2/(1+x^4). By symmetry, the integral over [-1/2,1/2] equals twice the integral over [0,1/2], giving option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\frac{(-x)^{2}}{1+(-x)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall the following:

  • a function f(x) is even if f(−x)=f(x)

  • a function f(x) is odd if f(−x)=−f(x)

Moreover, for any even function f(x), the graph of y=f(x) is symmetric across the y-axis, so we have ∫−aaf(x)dx=2∫0af(x)dx.

Notice that f(x)=x21+x4 is an even function. Indeed, we have f(−x)=(−x)21+(−x)4=x21+x4=f(x).

So, because f(x)=x21+x4 is an even function, we have ∫−1/21/2x21+x4dx=2∫01/2x21+x4dx.

content.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\frac{(-x)^{2}}{1+(-x)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-2}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-3}^{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{4}4\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)={sin}^{2}⁡x$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & ={sin}^{2}⁡(-x) \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(2(-x)) \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x) \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)=4\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}h(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

decision.explanation: Writing the integrand as f(x)=2^x-2^{-x}, we have f(-x)=2^{-x}-2^x=-f(x). It is continuous and odd, so its integral over [-2,2] is zero.

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}})$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =({2}^{(-x)}-\frac{1}{{2}^{(-x)}}) \\  & =({(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}-\frac{1}{(1/2)^{x}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{2}^{x}}-{2}^{x}) \\  & =-({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}}) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}})$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Simplify the integral ∫−22(2x−12x)dx using symmetry.

a
2∫02(2x−12x)dx
b
12∫02(2x−12x)dx
c
−∫02(2x−12x)dx
d
0

∫02(2x−12x)dx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall the following:

  • a function f(x) is even if f(−x)=f(x)

  • a function f(x) is odd if f(−x)=−f(x)

Moreover, for any odd function f(x), the graph of y=f(x) has rotational symmetry of order 2 about the origin, so we have ∫−aaf(x)dx=0.

Notice that f(x)=(2x−12x) is an odd function. Indeed, we have

f(−x)=(2(−x)−12(−x))=((12)x−1(1/2)x)=(12x−2x)=−(2x−12x)=−f(x).

So, because f(x)=(2x−12x) is an odd function, we have ∫−22(2x−12x)dx=0.

content.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}})$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =({2}^{(-x)}-\frac{1}{{2}^{(-x)}}) \\  & =({(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}-\frac{1}{(1/2)^{x}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{2}^{x}}-{2}^{x}) \\  & =-({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}}) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}})$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}({2}^{x}-\frac{1}{{2}^{x}})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

decision.explanation: The integrand is odd because (-x)e^{(-x)^4}=-xe^{x^4}. Its integral over the symmetric interval [-1,1] is therefore zero.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x){e}^{(-x)^{4}} \\  & =-x{e}^{{x}^{4}} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}x{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Question 15
?

Simplify the integral ∫−11xex4dx using symmetry.

a
4∫01xex4dx
b
−∫01xex4dx
c
−4∫01xex4dx
d
0
e
12∫01xex4dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the following:

  • a function f(x) is even if f(−x)=f(x)

  • a function f(x) is odd if f(−x)=−f(x)

Moreover, for any odd function f(x), the graph of y=f(x) has rotational symmetry of order 2 about the origin, so we have ∫−aaf(x)dx=0.

Notice that f(x)=xex4 is an odd function. Indeed, we have

f(−x)=(−x)e(−x)4=−xex4=−f(x).

So, because f(x)=xex4 is an odd function, we have ∫−11xex4dx=0.

content.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x){e}^{(-x)^{4}} \\  & =-x{e}^{{x}^{4}} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}x{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$
